title: Shavuot
hookLine: the day the Torah was given, kept with all-night study and the book of Ruth

cards: It's one in the morning, and the synagogue lights are still on. The room is full, and nobody's praying yet. They're studying.
Pairs of people bent over books, arguing gently. A teacher at the front with a room of teenagers. Someone's brought a thermos of coffee and a plate of cheesecake.
A few people are dozing on the benches. They'll stay until the sky starts to lighten, then pray the morning service at dawn. On this night, staying awake is the whole point.

teach.b: The holiday is Shavuot, which means weeks: the seven weeks just counted.

teach.h: A HARVEST, AND THE GIFT AT SINAI.
teach.b: In the Torah itself, Shavuot is a harvest festival, the day an offering from the new wheat was brought, the day of first fruits. The Torah never says anything else happened on this day. But the rabbis did the math.

The Torah says the Israelites reached Mount Sinai in the third month after leaving Egypt, and in the Talmud the sages reckon that the Ten Commandments were given on the sixth of that month, which is Shavuot; one rabbi says the seventh.
So in Jewish tradition, Shavuot became the time of the giving of the Torah, the gift at the mountain.
One reason given for the all-night study is a midrash: on the morning the Torah was given, the Israelites overslept, and Moses had to wake them.
Later, Jewish mystics made a practice of staying up all night on Shavuot, to be awake this time, and the custom spread. It's called a tikkun, a repair. Then there's Ruth.
On Shavuot, the book of Ruth is read, a harvest story set during the barley and wheat harvests.

Ruth, a woman from Moab, chooses to stay with her mother-in-law Naomi and join her people: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."

teach.h: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.
teach.b: One reason given for reading it today: it's the story of someone freely accepting the Torah, as Israel did at Sinai. And Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
There's also a custom of eating dairy foods; the reasons given vary, and no one reason is certain.

how: On Shavuot, many Jews stay up all night studying Torah (Tikkun Leil Shavuot), pray at dawn, read the Ten Commandments and the book of Ruth in synagogue, and eat dairy foods.

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband has died, and your mother-in-law Naomi tells you to go back to your own people. what do you do?
o: go home to Moab, as she says.
stay with Naomi and go with her.
stay in Moab but promise to visit.
games.why: Ruth refuses to leave: whither thou goest, I will go. tradition reads her choice as freely accepting the Torah, as Israel did at Sinai.

practice: Think of the gifts you've been given that you almost slept through: a teacher, a conversation, a book someone pressed into your hands. Pick one, and stay awake with it a little longer, as if this time you won't sleep through it.

wordCard.voice: Shavuot. Weeks: the festival fifty days after Passover, a wheat harvest, and the time Jews remember the giving of the Torah.

orig.note: Hebrew: weeks; the festival seven weeks after Passover.

carryVoice: Your line: stay up for the gift. Every year, on the fiftieth day, the gift comes round again. Until tomorrow.
